screens.title: Building an ERC-721 NFT Contract
screens.subtitle: Create unique, verifiable digital assets using OpenZeppelin, IPFS, and Hardhat

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn to build a production-friendly ERC-721 contract and link its tokens to immutable metadata. We'll use Hardhat and OpenZeppelin to avoid reinventing standard behavior, and we'll store images and metadata on IPFS so token URIs remain decentralized. You will see the full flow: initialize a project, author a MyNFT. sol contract that uses Counters and Ownable, prepare images and metadata, upload a metadata folder to IPFS to produce a base CID, then deploy and mint on a testnet and verify tokenURIs. This matters because NFTs are only valuable when ownership, provenance, and metadata are reliable. A common pitfall is using mutable HTTP URLs for asset links or leaving minting open to the public. Throughout the screens you'll find concrete code examples you can copy into your Hardhat project, a deployment script to run on Sepolia, and step checks to verify your metadata resolves correctly. By the end you'll be able to deploy, mint, and confirm ownership and metadata on-chain and off-chain—readying your collection for marketplaces or tests. What unique use will you build with your first NFT?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Use OpenZeppelin ERC-721 plus Counters and Ownable, host assets & metadata on IPFS, and deploy with Hardhat so minted NFTs resolve to immutable metadata and controlled supply.

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to set up a Hardhat project and install OpenZeppelin, implement a minimal but secure ERC-721 contract using Counters and Ownable, prepare and upload assets and metadata to IPFS, and deploy and interact with your contract on a testnet. Each objective ties a practical skill to an outcome: a running contract, minted tokens, and verifiable metadata. For example, setting up the environment means you can run a deploy script that mints the first token to your account. Implementing the contract ensures only authorized accounts can mint and that token URIs resolve to immutable metadata. Uploading to IPFS preserves asset integrity for marketplaces and verification steps. Finally, deploying to a testnet and verifying tokens teaches you the full lifecycle from code to on-chain evidence. These skills are immediately useful for building a collectible series, proof-of-ownership system, or any application where unique digital items are required. As you complete each objective, you accumulate a verified milestone you can demo to others.

screens.title: MyNFT.sol: inheritance and core contract structure
screens.subtitle: ERC721, Ownable, and Counters explained with the contract skeleton

narration.text: A secure NFT contract uses proven building blocks. In our MyNFT. sol we inherit from OpenZeppelin's ERC721 for token semantics and Ownable for access control. We use Counters. Counter to generate sequential tokenIds. The constructor accepts a name, symbol, and baseTokenURI so the contract knows how to resolve tokenURIs. We override the internal _baseURI() function to return the stored _baseTokenURI so tokenURI(tokenId) concatenates the base and id. A concrete example: calling the constructor with name "Cohortia NFT", symbol "CNFT" and an IPFS base URI means tokenURI(0) will resolve to ipfs:// /0. A common misconception is that ERC721 automatically stores metadata; it does not — tokenURI logic depends on _baseURI. Another mistake is initializing Ownable incorrectly; pass the deployer address so onlyOwner checks behave as expected. The contract skeleton also includes setBaseURI so the owner can update metadata pointers, and comments suggest adding Pausable for emergency pauses. Understanding these relationships keeps minting safe and metadata resolvable. MyNFT.sol: inheritance and core contract structure means erc721 provides token behavior, ownable restricts actions to the deployer, and counters ensures unique tokenids; _baseuri ties tokens to ipfs metadata.. In practical terms, erc721, ownable, and counters explained with the contract skeleton. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Contract anatomy
keyIdea.text: ERC721 provides token behavior, Ownable restricts actions to the deployer, and Counters ensures unique tokenIds; _baseURI ties tokens to IPFS metadata.

content.html:
Definition
Contract skeleton with core imports
MyNFT.sol (excerpt)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

import "@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC721/ERC721.sol";
import "@openzeppelin/contracts/access/Ownable.sol";
import "@openzeppelin/contracts/utils/Counters.sol";

contract MyNFT is ERC721, Ownable {
  using Counters for Counters.Counter;
  Counters.Counter private _tokenIdCounter;

  string private _baseTokenURI;

  constructor(string memory name_, string memory symbol_, string memory baseTokenURI_)
    ERC721(name_, symbol_)
    Ownable(msg.sender)
  {
    _baseTokenURI = baseTokenURI_;
  }

  function _baseURI() internal view override returns (string memory) {
    return _baseTokenURI;
  }

  function setBaseURI(string memory baseTokenURI_) public onlyOwner {
    _baseTokenURI = baseTokenURI_;
  }
}
Explanation cards
Counters.Counter
Provides safe incrementing tokenIds; avoids collisions when minting sequential tokens.
Ownable
Restricts sensitive functions like mint and setBaseURI to the contract owner to protect supply and metadata.
_baseURI()
Returns the base URI used by tokenURI to compose the metadata location for each tokenId.

screens.title: Minting and tokenId management
screens.subtitle: How safeMint, Counters, and onlyOwner work together

narration.text: Minting is where contract design meets supply control. In MyNFT the safeMint function uses Counters to obtain a newItemId, increments the counter, then calls _safeMint(to, newItemId). The _safeMint variant includes a check for contracts implementing ERC721TokenReceiver so tokens aren't accidentally locked in contracts that don't accept them. The function is protected by onlyOwner which means only the deployer or an authorized account can mint. A concrete example: if the current counter is 0, calling safeMint(deployerAddress) returns newItemId 0, increments the counter to 1, and assigns token 0 to the deployer. A common misconception is thinking anyone can mint; removing onlyOwner would allow arbitrary minting and destroy scarcity. Another nuance is whether tokenId starts at 0 or 1; Counters starts at 0 unless adjusted. Be intentional about which ids you expose in metadata naming. Also consider adding pausable behavior for emergencies; pausing transfers or minting protects against discovered vulnerabilities. The primary takeaway is: minting must be authorized, use _safeMint for safety, and manage tokenIds predictably so metadata lines up with tokens. Minting and tokenId management means use _safemint with counters for unique tokenids and onlyowner to protect supply; confirm index origin and metadata naming conventions.. In practical terms, how safemint, counters, and onlyowner work together. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Minting rules
keyIdea.text: Use _safeMint with Counters for unique tokenIds and onlyOwner to protect supply; confirm index origin and metadata naming conventions.

content.html:
Process Flow
safeMint lifecycle
safeMint example
function safeMint(address to) public onlyOwner {
  uint256 newItemId = _tokenIdCounter.current();
  _tokenIdCounter.increment();
  _safeMint(to, newItemId);
}
This flow gets a current id, increments for the next call, and mints safely to the recipient. Note that _safeMint performs a receiver check to avoid sending NFTs into contracts that can’t handle them.
Quick notes
  • onlyOwner: prevents open minting by anyone.
  • Counters start at 0 by default; decide if you want 0 or 1 as the first tokenId.
  • _safeMint vs _mint: prefer _safeMint for transfer safety when recipients might be contracts.
  • Consider pause functionality for emergency response.

screens.title: Base URI and tokenURI composition
screens.subtitle: How the contract resolves token metadata URIs

narration.text: The base URI is the contract's pointer to where token metadata lives. In MyNFT we store _baseTokenURI and override _baseURI() to return it. When tokenURI(tokenId) is called, the ERC-721 implementation concatenates the base and the tokenId to produce a complete URI. For example, if _baseTokenURI is ipfs://QmBaseCID/ then tokenURI(1) becomes ipfs://QmBaseCID/1. It is essential to include the trailing slash in the base when your metadata files are named 0. json, 1. json, etc.; missing the slash is a common error that yields invalid URIs like ipfs://QmBaseCID1. A second subtlety is mutable vs immutable storage: storing HTTP links undercuts decentralization, so prefer ipfs:// links for permanence. The contract also exposes setBaseURI to update the base when needed, but changing it after minting should be deliberate because it affects what tokenURIs resolve to. A good practice is to perform metadata reveals by changing the base once, rather than hosting mutable file contents at the target URIs. The main takeaway is that correctly formatted baseTokenURI plus consistent metadata filenames ensures tokenURI resolves reliably. Base URI and tokenURI composition means _tokenuri uses the contract's base uri plus tokenid; include a trailing slash and prefer ipfs:// to keep metadata immutable.. In practical terms, how the contract resolves token metadata uris. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: URI mechanics
keyIdea.text: _tokenURI uses the contract's base URI plus tokenId; include a trailing slash and prefer ipfs:// to keep metadata immutable.

content.html:
Definition
tokenURI composition
_baseTokenURI example
_baseTokenURI = "ipfs://Qm...metadataBaseCID.../"; // tokenURI(0) -> ipfs://Qm...metadataBaseCID.../0
Always test tokenURI after deployment and open it in an IPFS gateway to confirm the JSON loads and references the expected image CID.
Pitfalls & guidance
  • Missing trailing slash: concatenate carefully to avoid malformed URIs.
  • Mutable HTTP URLs: avoid if you need permanent provenance.
  • Changing baseTokenURI after mint: can be used for reveals, but document the change and reason.

screens.title: Prepare assets and metadata JSON
screens.subtitle: Create image files and standards-compliant JSON metadata

narration.text: Preparing metadata is a simple but structured task. First, create your image files like nft0. png and nft1. png and keep them in a local assets folder. Next, for each token create a JSON file that follows the ERC-721 metadata format: include name, description, image pointing to an ipfs:// CID for the uploaded image, and any attributes. For example, 1. json might include an image field ipfs://QmImageCID. A concrete example JSON contains a name, description, image, and attributes with trait_type and value. After creating images and JSON locally, upload each image to IPFS and note their CIDs. Then place the JSON files in a directory and upload that directory to IPFS so you get one base CID for all metadata files. A frequent mistake is placing HTTP asset links inside image fields instead of IPFS URIs; that undermines immutability. Also ensure the names of your JSON files match the tokenIds your contract will produce. This mapping is critical: tokenId 0 must have 0. json in metadata if you use zero-based ids. Validate one tokenURI locally in an IPFS gateway before deploying to catch mismatches early.

keyIdea.title: Metadata process
keyIdea.text: Create images and JSON files, upload images to IPFS to get image CIDs, then upload the metadata directory to IPFS to obtain a base CID for the contract.

content.html:
Process
Assets → metadata → base CID
Example metadata file (1.json)
{
  "name": "My NFT #1",
  "description": "The first NFT in my Cohortia collection.",
  "image": "ipfs://Qm...image1CID...",
  "attributes": [
    { "trait_type": "Edition", "value": "1/100" }
  ]
}
Make sure the image field uses the IPFS CID returned when you upload the actual image file.
Checklist before upload
  • Match file names to tokenIds (0.json, 1.json).
  • Ensure image values point to ipfs://CIDs not HTTP placeholders.
  • Keep attribute schema consistent across items for marketplace compatibility.
  • Test one tokenURI in an IPFS gateway to confirm the image loads.

screens.title: Upload metadata directory and set baseTokenURI
screens.subtitle: Get a single CID for all metadata files and update your contract

narration.text: Uploading metadata as a directory yields a single base CID you can set on the contract. Use Pinata or the IPFS CLI to upload images individually and then upload the metadata folder containing 0. json, 1. json, etc. Pinata returns one CID that identifies the directory root. That CID becomes ipfs:// / which you pass into MyNFT's constructor as baseTokenURI. A concrete example: after uploading metadata/, Pinata returns QmMetadataCID and you construct baseTokenURI as ipfs://QmMetadataCID/. Deploy the contract initialized with that base and then call tokenURI(0) to confirm it resolves to ipfs://QmMetadataCID/0. Common mistakes include uploading files to different folders or forgetting to include a trailing slash; either will break resolution. Another issue is pinning: ensure files are pinned so they remain accessible. Finally, when updating baseTokenURI later with setBaseURI, remember that already minted tokenURIs will change how they resolve, so document any intentional reveals or updates. Getting the base CID right is critical for on-chain to off-chain mapping. Upload metadata directory and set baseTokenURI means a single metadata directory cid becomes the contract basetokenuri, so upload consistently, pin assets, and confirm tokenuri resolution after deployment.. In practical terms, get a single cid for all metadata files and update your contract. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Base CID importance
keyIdea.text: A single metadata directory CID becomes the contract baseTokenURI, so upload consistently, pin assets, and confirm tokenURI resolution after deployment.

content.html:
Process
Directory upload → baseTokenURI
Upload steps
  1. Upload images and copy their CIDs into the respective JSON files.
  2. Place JSON files in a metadata/ directory and upload that directory to Pinata or IPFS CLI.
  3. Capture the returned CID and form baseTokenURI as ipfs://<CID>/
  4. Use that baseTokenURI when deploying MyNFT so tokenURI resolves correctly.
Common mistakes
  • Forgetting the trailing slash when your files are named by number.
  • Uploading inconsistent file names so tokenIds don't map to files.
  • Not pinning files leading to eventual unavailability.

screens.title: Deploy script walkthrough
screens.subtitle: A Hardhat deploy script that deploys and mints sample NFTs

narration.text: Your deploy script wires everything together. It creates a MyNFT contract instance with name, symbol, and the baseTokenURI you got from IPFS. After deployment, the script mints tokens to the deployer and optionally to other test addresses to demonstrate transfer and ownership. A concrete deploy example prints the deployed address, deployer balance, mints token 0 to the deployer, and token 1 to a second test account. Errors to watch for include passing an incorrect baseTokenURI or forgetting to await transaction receipts before calling ownerOf or tokenURI. Also ensure hardhat. config. js is configured with the correct network and private key referenced from. env. Running npx hardhat run scripts/deployNFT. js --network sepolia performs the deployment. After the script completes, check Etherscan to confirm contract address, then call tokenURI(0) and ownerOf(0) to verify. This script both demonstrates the end-to-end flow and provides an automated way to produce initial tokens for verification and testing. Deploy script walkthrough means a deployment script should deploy with basetokenuri, mint initial tokens, wait for receipts, and print addresses and tokenuris for verification.. In practical terms, a hardhat deploy script that deploys and mints sample nfts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Deployment pattern
keyIdea.text: A deployment script should deploy with baseTokenURI, mint initial tokens, wait for receipts, and print addresses and tokenURIs for verification.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
deployNFT.js example
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

async function main() {
  const [deployer] = await ethers.getSigners();

  console.log("Deploying contracts with the account:", deployer.address);

  const baseTokenURI = "ipfs://Qm...metadataBaseCID.../";

  const MyNFT = await ethers.getContractFactory("MyNFT");
  const myNFT = await MyNFT.deploy("Cohortia NFT", "CNFT", baseTokenURI);

  await myNFT.waitForDeployment();

  console.log("MyNFT deployed to:", myNFT.target);

  console.log("Minting NFT #0 to deployer...");
  const mintTx = await myNFT.safeMint(deployer.address);
  await mintTx.wait();
  console.log("NFT #0 minted. Owner:", await myNFT.ownerOf(0));
  console.log("Token URI for #0:", await myNFT.tokenURI(0));
}

main().catch((error) => { console.error(error); process.exit(1); });
Remember to replace baseTokenURI with your actual CID and configure hardhat.config.js and .env for the target network and private key.

Another verification is marketplace indexing; some platforms index testnet NFTs after a delay, so don't expect immediate appearance. Practical tip: keep the deployer address visible and log balances to confirm you had enough testnet funds for deployment. This verification loop confirms the mapping from on-chain tokenId to off-chain metadata and proves your contract functions in a live environment. Process
Deployment verification
Steps after deployment
  1. Find the contract address output by the script and open the network Etherscan.
  2. Call ownerOf(0) and tokenURI(0) from the Read Contract tab.
  3. Open the value of tokenURI in an IPFS gateway to view the JSON and image.

Troubleshooting

  • Image not loading: confirm image CID in the JSON points to the correct image CID.
  • Mint tx pending: ensure you await receipts before calling ownerOf in scripts.

screens.title: Common mistakes and security considerations
screens.subtitle: What to avoid and how to harden your NFT contract

narration.text: Two recurring mistakes undermine NFT projects: open mint functions and mutable metadata links. If safeMint lacks onlyOwner, anyone can inflate supply and devalue the collection. Always gate mint functions with access control—Ownable is a simple choice but role-based patterns may suit more complex flows. Mutable metadata—hosting images or JSON on HTTP endpoints you control—allows content to change and breaks the guarantee of immutability. Prefer IPFS CIDs to keep assets content-addressed. Another security idea is adding Pausable to allow emergency suspension of transfers or minting. A more advanced approach is using role-based AccessControl to delegate minting privileges to specific addresses instead of a single owner. Testing considerations include writing unit tests to assert onlyOwner behavior, verifying tokenURI string formatting, and simulating pause/unpause behavior. Finally, document any allowed metadata updates in your project's governance or roadmap so collectors know when and why a baseTokenURI might change. The main defense is explicit, minimal, and testable permissioning plus immutable asset hosting. Common mistakes and security considerations means never leave minting open to everyone; prefer ipfs-hosted metadata; add pausable and test access control to protect your collection.. In practical terms, what to avoid and how to harden your nft contract. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avoid these errors
keyIdea.text: Never leave minting open to everyone; prefer IPFS-hosted metadata; add pausable and test access control to protect your collection.

content.html:
Comparison
Security patterns
Open mint vs onlyOwner
Open mint allows unlimited tokens to be created by anyone and destroys scarcity. Using onlyOwner or AccessControl restricts minting to trusted accounts and preserves intended supply and provenance.
Mutable HTTP vs IPFS
HTTP URLs can be changed or taken down. IPFS CIDs are content-addressed and preserve the exact file; prefer ipfs:// URIs in your metadata for permanence.
Pausable & testing
Pausable lets owners suspend operations in emergencies. Write unit tests to assert onlyOwner, pause/unpause, and tokenURI correctness before deploying.
Pro tip
Document any intended metadata updates as part of your minting policy so collectors understand when reveals or base URI changes may occur.

screens.title: Minting and viewing your first NFT (lab)
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step lab to mint, view, and transfer NFTs on Sepolia

narration.text: This lab walks you through minting and verifying two NFTs. First prepare two images nft0. png and nft1. png and upload them to Pinata or IPFS CLI. Copy the two image CIDs into 0. json and 1. json, then upload the metadata folder and capture its base CID. Update your deployNFT. js baseTokenURI with ipfs://yourMetadataBaseCID/ and run npx hardhat run scripts/deployNFT. js --network sepolia. The script will deploy MyNFT, mint NFT #0 to the deployer, and mint NFT #1 to another test account if included. After deployment, copy the contract address and open Sepolia Etherscan. In the read contract tab call ownerOf(0) and tokenURI(0); open the tokenURI in an IPFS gateway to view the metadata and image. Finally, use the write contract tab or a simple script to call safeTransferFrom or transferFrom to move an NFT to another account and confirm ownerOf reflects the change. A common error here is not waiting for transactions to be mined before reading state; always await receipts. This hands-on loop ensures you can produce, verify, and transfer NFTs end-to-end.
